sections.title: Evolution of deployment and components of ML deployment
sections.plain: From apps on bare servers to orchestrated containers; ML deployment needs packaging, serving, scaling and MLOps.
sections.body:
Evolution: traditional (apps on an OS on hardware) → virtualised (a hypervisor runs VMs, each with a guest OS) → containers (a container engine on one OS) → Kubernetes (orchestrating many containers across nodes).

ML deployment: integrating a trained model into production so it predicts on live, unseen data, usually accessed via REST or gRPC, and scalable, reliable, secure and monitored.

ComponentWhat it covers
Packaging and containerisationModel, weights, dependencies, runtime and preprocessing bundled in a Docker image
ServingREST/gRPC endpoints (FastAPI, Flask)
Scalability and orchestrationKubernetes: horizontal pod autoscaling, load balancing, self-healing, rolling updates
MLOpsVersioning, CI/CD, automated tests and deployment, monitoring, logging, retraining

sections.title: Containers and why they exist
sections.plain: Bring your own microphone and speakers: package the environment with the app.
sections.body:
Singer analogy: at concert 1 the venue's microphone fails, at concert 2 the speakers; so the singer brings their own mike and speakers. Software moves through dev, test, certification and production environments, and "we can't replicate the production issue in dev" is the classic symptom of environments differing.

A container is a standardised package containing code, runtime, system libraries and settings: build, ship and run anywhere. Docker containers are lightweight, portable and self-sufficient.

ContainersVirtual machines
Share the host OS kernel; no guest OSEach VM runs a full guest OS on a hypervisor
Lightweight (MBs), start in secondsHeavy (GBs), start in minutes
Process-level isolationStronger isolation (separate kernels)

sections.title: Docker: Dockerfile, image, container
sections.plain: A Dockerfile is the recipe, an image is the packaged meal, a container is the meal being eaten.
sections.body:
Dockerfile: the blueprint, a text file of instructions. Image: a template; a standalone executable package (code, runtime, libraries, tools) built in read-only layers. Container: a running process of an image; one image can start many containers.

Purpose: reproduce identical dev, staging and production environments; share images via registries with docker push / docker pull. Architecture: the client (docker build, pull, run) talks via a REST API to the Docker daemon on the Docker host, which manages images and containers and exchanges images with a registry (Docker Hub hosts official images; Docker Desktop provides a GUI).

KeywordPurpose
FROMBase image
RUNExecute a command at build time (creates a layer)
COPY / ADDCopy files into the image (ADD also handles URLs and archives)
WORKDIRSet working directory
ENVEnvironment variables
EXPOSEDocument the listening port
CMD / ENTRYPOINTDefault command / fixed executable when the container starts
USER, VOLUME, LABELRun-as user, persistent mount points, metadata (LABEL replaces deprecated MAINTAINER)
FROM ubuntu:latest
RUN mkdir /vim
RUN apt update
RUN apt install vim -y
WORKDIR /vim
ENTRYPOINT ["/bin/bash"]

docker build -t myimg . creates the layered image; docker run myimg starts a container.

sections.title: Containerising an ML model
sections.plain: Put the model file, the API code, its dependencies and config in one image.
sections.body:
What goes in: the model file (.pkl, .onnx, .pt, .h5), inference code/API, dependencies, runtime, configuration, and pre/post-processing.

Demo layout: model.pkl, train.py, app.py (FastAPI), preprocess.py, postprocess.py, requirements.txt, Dockerfile, config.yaml.

Flow
  1. Train a RandomForest on Iris; save model.pkl.
  2. docker build -t iris-model .
  3. docker run -p 8000:8000 iris-model
  4. POST /predict with sepal_length, sepal_width, petal_length, petal_width.
  5. Pre-process JSON → NumPy 1×4 array → predict → post-process index → class name.
  6. Response {"prediction": 0, "class": "setosa"}.

Code example ex1 runs exactly this service in-process and prints the Dockerfile; copying requirements.txt before the code keeps the dependency layer cached.

sections.title: Kubernetes: features and architecture
sections.plain: A control plane decides where containers run; worker nodes run them and keep them healthy.
sections.body:
Kubernetes: open-source container orchestration, originally from Google, donated to the CNCF (its first project to graduate, 2018), written in Go. Features: high availability, scalability, disaster recovery. Managed offerings: Amazon EKS, Google GKE, Azure AKS.

Cluster: users drive it through kubectl (or a UI) → the master (control plane) → worker nodes. Pods are the smallest deployable units: a group of containers sharing storage and network, with their own IP.

Control planeRole
API serverCentral control point; persists state to etcd
etcdDistributed key-value store: the source of truth
Controller managerReplicaSet controller (replica counts), Deployment controller (rolling updates)
SchedulerPlaces pods by resource requirements, node availability and policies (prefers a 40%-full node over an 80%-full one)
Worker sideRole
kubeletNode agent: keeps containers running and healthy, restarts them
kube-proxyNetworking for services
Container runtimeRuns containers

Other key objects: services (stable IP/DNS for a group of pods) and controllers (maintain desired replica counts).

sections.title: Pods, Deployments and YAML
sections.plain: Declare what you want in YAML; Kubernetes makes it so.
sections.body:
Abstraction layers: a Deployment manages a ReplicaSet, which manages Pods; a Pod abstracts one or more containers. A Deployment is a template for pods, written in YAML.

apiVersion: v1                 apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Pod                      kind: Deployment
metadata:                      metadata:
  name: my-pod                   name: my-app
spec:                          spec:
  containers:                    replicas: 2
  - name: my-cont                selector:
    image: nginx:latest            matchLabels: {app: my-app}
                                 template:
                                   metadata:
                                     labels: {app: my-app}
                                   spec:
                                     containers:
                                     - name: my-cont
                                       image: nginx:latest

Apply with kubectl apply -f pod-definition.yaml. (An apps/v1 Deployment requires spec.selector.matchLabels matching the template's labels.)

Minikube demo: build the iris-model image locally → start Minikube → minikube image load iris-model → write the deployment YAML → kubectl apply → 2 FastAPI pods running → kubectl port-forward 8000:8000 → open /docs → POST /predict → {"prediction": 0, "class": "setosa"}. Code example ex2 generates such a manifest and simulates scheduling and self-healing.

sections.title: CI/CD lifecycle with GitOps
sections.plain: CI builds and tests; Git declares what runs; a CD agent syncs the cluster.
sections.body:
1. Developer pushes to the source code repository (Git).
  2. CI pipeline (Jenkins, GitHub Actions) tests and builds the image.
  3. Image pushed to an image registry (Docker Hub).
  4. CI updates the deployment configuration in a separate deployment repository (Helm/Kustomize manifests): GitOps.
  5. A CD pipeline (Argo CD) pulls the change.
  6. It syncs the Kubernetes cluster and reports sync status.

Because the desired state lives in Git, every deployment is reviewed, auditable and reversible by reverting a commit. (An end-to-end DevOps demo is provided for self-study.)

sections.title: Further insights and misconceptions
sections.body:
• Avoid :latest in production manifests; pin immutable tags or digests so rollbacks are exact.
  • Resource requests and limits let the scheduler pack pods correctly and prevent one model from starving others.
  • Liveness and readiness probes tell Kubernetes when to restart a pod and when it can receive traffic (e.g. after the model has loaded).
  • GPUs are requested as resources (nvidia.com/gpu: 1) and need device plugins on nodes.

code.title: The containerised iris model service
code.explain: Trains and saves model.pkl, serves POST /predict with pre-processing to a 1×4 array and post-processing to a class name, and prints the Dockerfile plus build/run commands.
mistakes: Loading the model on every request.
Copying code before installing requirements (slow rebuilds).
code.notes: With Docker installed: docker build -t iris-model . && docker run -p 8000:8000 iris-model.
code.code:
"""The iris model service that goes into a Docker image: train -> save -> serve.

train() fits a RandomForest and saves model.pkl; app exposes POST /predict with
pre-processing (JSON -> 1x4 NumPy array) and post-processing (index -> class name).
We call it in-process with TestClient, then print the Dockerfile and the commands
that would build and run the container.
"""
import pickle, tempfile, os
import numpy as np
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
from pydantic import BaseModel
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier

WORKDIR = tempfile.mkdtemp(); MODEL_PATH = os.path.join(WORKDIR, "model.pkl")
iris = load_iris()

def train():                                                    # train.py
    clf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=50, random_state=0).fit(iris.data, iris.target)
    with open(MODEL_PATH, "wb") as f: pickle.dump(clf, f)
    return os.path.getsize(MODEL_PATH)

class IrisIn(BaseModel):
    sepal_length: float; sepal_width: float; petal_length: float; petal_width: float

def preprocess(x: IrisIn) -> np.ndarray:                       # preprocess.py
    return np.array([[x.sepal_length, x.sepal_width, x.petal_length, x.petal_width]])

def postprocess(idx: int) -> dict:                              # postprocess.py
    return {"prediction": int(idx), "class": str(iris.target_names[idx])}

print(f"model.pkl written ({train():,} bytes)")
app = FastAPI(title="iris-model")                               # app.py
with open(MODEL_PATH, "rb") as f: MODEL = pickle.load(f)        # loaded once at start-up

@app.post("/predict")
def predict(x: IrisIn):
    arr = preprocess(x)
    return postprocess(MODEL.predict(arr)[0])

c = TestClient(app)
for body in [{"sepal_length": 5.1, "sepal_width": 3.5, "petal_length": 1.4, "petal_width": 0.2},
             {"sepal_length": 6.7, "sepal_width": 3.0, "petal_length": 5.2, "petal_width": 2.3}]:
    print("POST /predict", body, "->", c.post("/predict", json=body).json())

DOCKERFILE = """FROM python:3.11-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY model.pkl app.py preprocess.py postprocess.py config.yaml ./
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["uvicorn", "app:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]"""
print("\nDockerfile:\n" + DOCKERFILE)
print("\nbuild & run:\n  docker build -t iris-model .\n  docker run -p 8000:8000 iris-model\n  curl -X POST localhost:8000/predict -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{...}'")
layers = [l.split()[0] for l in DOCKERFILE.splitlines() if l.split()[0] in ("FROM", "RUN", "COPY")]
print(f"\nfilesystem layers created by: {layers}; requirements are copied before code so code edits reuse the cached pip layer")

POST /predict {'sepal_length': 5.1, 'sepal_width': 3.5, 'petal_length': 1.4, 'petal_width': 0.2} -> {'prediction': 0, 'class': 'setosa'}
POST /predict {'sepal_length': 6.7, 'sepal_width': 3.0, 'petal_length': 5.2, 'petal_width': 2.3} -> {'prediction': 2, 'class': 'virginica'}

Dockerfile:

WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY model.pkl app.py preprocess.py postprocess.py config.yaml ./
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["uvicorn", "app:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]

build & run:

  docker run -p 8000:8000 iris-model
  curl -X POST localhost:8000/predict -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{...}'

code.title: A Deployment manifest and a toy control loop
code.explain: Generates an apps/v1 Deployment YAML, then simulates scheduling on the least-loaded node, replacing a crashed pod, rescheduling after a node failure, scaling up and running out of capacity (Pending).
mistakes: No resource requests, so scheduling is blind.
code.notes: Real clusters: kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml; kubectl get pods -o wide; kubectl scale deployment iris-model --replicas=6.
